WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 88 to provide for the appointment of a Tariff Commission. He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of this Bill to create a Tariff Commission, I am sure I need not say that it is not the intention of the government to delegate or attempt to delegate its powers and functions with regard to the making of tariffs to any outside body. Under our parliamentary system, the duty of originating Bills for the raising of revenue devolves upon the government, and the responsibility for such Bills must remain with the government. Under this proposed Act creating a Tariff Commission, the duty and responsibility with respect to the tariff shall remain precisely as it is at present, precisely as it has been in the past. In this respect there is no departure whatever from the former practice. The wish has often been expressed that the tariff could be taken out of politics and that a commission akin to the Railway Commission might deal with it; a commission having power not only to obtain information but to actually fix tariff rates. The idea underlying this wish is, of course, that the tariff and the fixing of tariff rates might be removed from the sphere of political influence, or the sphere of_ party favouritism, and that a commission should fix the rates of the tarff upon a basis that would be fair, and just, and equitable to all classes of the community, producers, and consumers alike. Now, apart from the question of governmental responsibility for national expenditure and for the raising of revenues, such a proposal could only be regarded as Utopian, and impractical, because there is probably no question in the whole realm of political science upon which men and parties and economists have more widely or more earnestly differed than as to the principle upon which tariff rates should be based and established. There are those who are free traders, and who believe Mr. BORDEN.
in a tariff for revenue only, but they differ among themselves as to the particular commodities that should be taxed and as to the proportion of the tax that should be borne by the several classes of the community-I am not speaking particularly with regard to Canada now when I speak of free traders and those who believe in a tariff for revenue only. Then, there are those who are protectionists, and they differ among themselves as to the degree of protection that should be accorded and the extent of time and the period over which pr flection should extend. I think we may safely say-and I am sure it is not necessary to elaborate the point in a representative assembly of this kind-we may safely say that there is no matter in the realm of political science about which men and parties are more apt to differ than the question of the proper basis for, and the principle of establishing tariff rates. I think, therefore, we may assume in view of this and other considerations, that the tariff cannot 'be taken out of politics, that it is in reality the most vital and essential feature in politics, that it is, and probably always will be the chief topic of political discussion.	_
Now, in any modern society, the task of tariff making or of tariff revision, especially upon a comprehensive scale, is one of very great difficulty and complexity, involving, as an indispensable preliminary, a more or less exhaustive investigation into economic conditions. In other words, where the tariff is a tariff for revenue only, or partly for revenue and partly protective, its basis should be the ascertainment, as accurately as possible, of facts. Let me give a practical illustration. From day to day in my office, the tariff being in the Department of Finance, I have applications from business men, from manufacturers, from others throughout the community, with regard to the tariff. These applicants have, or fancy they have, some grievances; they either wish a higher degree of protection, or, some of them may complain, and they may justly complain, that the tariff unduly favours certain industries, that the rate of living has been unduly enhanced by reason thereof, and they ask that the matter be looked into. Now, Tight at the outset, and before that matter can be properly investigated, there comes up the question: what are the facts. In other words, tihe question of facts is an absolutely necessary preliminary to proper tariff investigation, and to proper and just tariff action. In Canada, with our vast extent of territory, with our great variety of resources, with our great industrial establishments, the task of tariff making is one of very great difficulty, a fact that has been recognized by previous governments whenever they have undertaken the task of tariff making

or tariff revision. They have tried to meet the situation by organizing committees or commissions-I prefer to call them committees, although they have been called by the ministers themselves commissions, they tried by this means to obtain the necessary facts and data upon which a tariff can only be justly and fairly and intelligently constructed. They have gone through the country, they have visited the principal places in Canada, and have there sought information. In 1893 a committee of the ministers of Sir John Thompson's Cabinet visited the principal centres of the Dominion for the purpose of obtaining information with a view to revise the tariff. In 1897, similarly, a committee of Cabinet ministers, three in number, visited the leading centres of the Dominion in quest of information. They gave hearings to parties who were desirous to be heard with regard to the tariff or who might have information useful to them in coming to a conclusion. In 1905 and 1906, similarly a committee of ministers visited various points of the Dominion, preparatory to the tariff legislation of 1907.
Now, Sir, I think that such committees would serve an extremely useful purpose. In the first place they would bring the ministers in touch with public opinion throughout the Dominion, the ministers would hear both sides, so to speak; they would hear the side of those in favour of an increase in the tariff or of maintaining the existing tariff, and they would hear, on the otheT hand, those who were opposed to such increase or such maintenance.
But I think it must be obvious to all that it would be absolutely impossible for such a committee of ministers visiting various parts of the Dominion to obtain anything like accurate statistical information, whieh I believe is indispensible to the making of a tariff upon a just and fair basis. It would be absolutely impossible for these ministers to obtain anything like accurate information with regard to the great variety of products and commodities mentioned in -the tariff schedules. Our customs revenue for the fiscal year ending the 31st of March, 1911, was over $73,000,000; our tariff Act embraces something like 740 different items; and these items in turn embrace thousands of commodities. One gets a fair idea from these figures of the great amount of information which would be necessary or desirable before anything like a comprehensive revision of the tariff could be attempted. I do not wish to overemphasize or to magnify the difficulty, because it is only fair to say that it is possible to become academic with regard to getting information; but there is no doubt that our tariff will be on a more just and equitable basis in proportion to the amount of accurate information w'hich we have at
hand at the time the tariff is created or is revised.
Other countries have been confronted with the same difficulty of obtaining facts as a preliminary to tariff action. Germany engaged some thirty experts for the purpose of obtaining information upon which her tariff might be based. Japan, preliminary to any tariff legislation, appoints a committee consisting of civil officials, members of parliament and leading business men, for the purpose of advising with regard to the items in the tariff schedules. The nearest approach to a permanent tariff commission, although it is not a tariff commission in the sense in which our Bill provides for one, is the Tariff Board of the United States. The Customs Tariff Act of the United States for the year 1909 contained maximum and minimum tariff provisions, and it left the administration of the tariff as to these maximum and minimum provisions in the hands of the President of the United States. The following provision was made in the Act:
To secure information to assist the President in the discharge of the duties imposed upon him by this section, and officers of the government in the administration of the customs laws, the President is hereby authorized to employ persons as may be required.
Subsequently he appointed three persons, the number being afterwards increased to five, to organize the bureau, and they were known as the Tariff Board. As to the duties of the board there is no definition in any statute, but the president of the board has thus defined them:
The duties of the board are the ascertainment of the difference in the cost of production at home and abroad and the ascertainment of the prices at home and abroad and their relation to local conditions.
The President desired to have the board made permanent, but in the meantime public sentiment had arisen calling for the creation of a Tariff Commission. In the United States there were two distinct notions prevalent as to the scope of this commission. One was that the commission should have the powers which I mentioned at the opening of my speech

that it should be absolutely independent of Congress with the power to fix the tariff rates. The other was that the commission should be auxiliary to the government, for the purpose of obtaining information on which tariff rates might be founded. A Bill was introduced founded on the latter conception, though slightly different in form, and passed both Houses, but failed of final enactment. It is generally acknowledged that the Tariff Board of the United States has performed very important and valuable services. Among the different works which if has undertaken I might mention

What ever criticism I might have to offer upon the Bill, the second reading of which has just been moved by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White, Leeds), no one can take exception to the clear explanation which he has given the House, of the proposal and his own intentions in regard to the proposal. As to much of what he has said, I can agree with him, and to many parts of his address I take no exception.
But I must disagree with him on the method he has adopted in seeking to obtain information and facts, which I believe all members of this House will deem t-o be necessary to enable us to bestow proper consideration upon any of the tariff questions which from time to time arise in this House. I object to the form in which the government has brought down this measure, and as I proceed, I think I can point out to the satisfaction of the House that the form is objectionable, and if persisted in, as brought before us in the shape of the present Bill, its operation and ultimate result will not only be objectionable, but I think I may go so far as to say may be disastrous to the great body of the citizens of this country.
I believe that the Finance Minister recognizes that this Bill is in the nature of a new departure. It is a radical departure from anything which we have hitherto known in our parliamentary or constitutional practice. In order to justify so radical a departure, strong reasons, substantial reasons, I think should have been given to the House. Mere matters of expediency are not sufficient for the purpose. Our constitutional practice, our parliamentary practice in respect to tariffs,
and in respect to the great question of national taxation, has not been the growth of a year, or of years, or of generations, but of centuries. It is the outcome of long centuries of ripe experience, and the rights which we in this parliament possess of dealing with matters of revenue and of taxation are rights not lightly to be interfered with, not lightly to be limited, and no government, I submit, is justified in raising any barrier between a government and the people who puts that government in power; and this Bill, in my opinion, raises at the outset such a barrier.
I think, too, that my hon. triend the Minister of Finance might at the outset have given the House some reason for bringing in this measure at the present session. What public demand has there been in Canada for such a measure? Has there been any demand? Has the question ever been discussed in this House or outside this House? Has it ever been discussed as a question of vital importance by the press of the country? I know, as every hon. member knows, that the question of the appointment of a tariff commission was raised by my right hon. friend, the leader of the government, in one or more than one of his many pre-election manifestos. But I know that I am quite within the mark when I say that the matter as a live issue was never discussed, either on the platform or in the press, and up till the present moment, so far as my knowledge goes, it has never been discussed in the parliament of Canada. Now what call or what demand has there been for such a measure? The Minister of Finance gave the House not a single instance of any demand, of any request, which had been made upon the government to formulate such a measure as that proposed in this Bill for the employment of a permanent tariff commission. We know that there is one important body in Canada that has called for it, and called loudly for it. We know that it has been a sort of an ideal of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association for a number of years back. We know that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association has year in and year out, in open session and in secret session, and at its banquets, announced its desire that a permanent tariff commission should be established in Canada. But apart from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, has any call come from any other section of the country? I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance:	Have any agricultural societies in Canada asked for the establishment of a permanent tariff commission? Have any of the dairymen's associations, any of the live stock associations, swine breeders' or sheep breeders' associations any western association, the Grain Growers' Association, the Dominion Grange-

have any of these men asked for it? Have any of the great consuming classes asked for such a measure? Has any request come from Boards of Trade? If so, the Minister of Finance did not give the House any information. Has he received requests from the great industrial classes, the Trade and Labour Congress, the trades unions, any of those representative bodies of the great consuming classes, have they made any request to the government, direct or indirect, that a permanent tariff commission should be established in Canada? I venture to say that, with the single exception of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, there has never been a request or a suggestion from any of the great public bodies in Canada for a Bill such as the one which is now under consideration.
Now, on the face of the Bill, one might suppose on a superficial glance, that it is perhaps innocuous, perhaps to some extent harmless. But I venture the assertion that any one who will carefully read the Bill, any one who will observe what I believe to be its real intent and purpose, will see that it is one of very far reaching scope, and of very serious consequence to the people of his country. It does, Sir, seem to me a strange thing that the first important official act, the first act, at all events, of any consequence or any magnitude, performed by the Minister of Finance in this House since his appointment to that high position a few months ago, should be the introduction of a Bill to establish a permanent tariff commission in Canada, a Bill which, on his own statement, both in foTm and in substance, I think I am safe in saying, is practically borrowed from the highest protectionist country in the world, from the United States of America. It is a strange comment, a strange sequel, upon events which happened just about a year ago in Massey hall, Toronto, at a tremendous gathering called by so-called Liberals to protest against the proposed reciprocity agreement with the United States. The hon. the Minister of Finance was on the platform at that gathering, and they tell me he made the best speech that was made on that occasion, and I am sure he would. His theme was that the United States systems are bad, their laws are bad, their methods, their manners are such as should not be adopted in Canada; they ' would lower us, they would not ennoble us. And now, Sir, we see that the first act of consequence or of magnitude, of that same hon. gentleman occupying the high position of Minister of Finance of Canada, is to bring in a Bill, to find a model for which he has gone across to Washington. He has culled the ' Con-Mr. GUTHRIE.
gressional Record ' of the United States Senate and House of Representatives, and he has brought here in concrete form what the high protectionist party in the United States deem a proper thing to safeguard high protection in that country.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, knows that he has perused that ' Congressional Record,' every page of it, dealing with this subject. I do not object to his doing so, but I say that his remarks are tainted with the arguments which were advanced by the high protectionist party in Congress for the passage of a similar measure. He will remember, as I do, that one member of the House of Representatives said: I support this -Bill because it is the best way to sustain the glorious doctrine of protection. That is one of the Tea-sons given in the House of Representatives and I, for one, have not a single doubt in my mind that the real object, purpose and intent of the present measure is to perpetuate and sustain, not the present system of protection, but a higher system of protection in the Dominion of Canada.
This Bill cannot be said to be original in any respect. There are only two or three countries, I believe, in the world-only two or three at all events, of which I know -which have adopted tariff commissions and it is a strange thing that the countries which have adopted this method of procedure, are the highest protected countries in the world. A tariff commission board seems to be a necessary adjunct to the high protective system, and I do not think I am going one jot beyond the truth when I say that this Bill is brought in here-almost the first important Bill of the first session of this parliament-as a quid pro quo for the Canadian Manufacturers' Association to redeem the promises made to them for their generous and lavish support during the election on the 21st day of September last.
Well, how will the Bill operate? Opinion may be divided upon that question and probably will. We have perhaps no plain statement of fact which you can lay before the House as to what will be the exact operation of the Bill and we cannot more than surmise what are the real intentions of the government in bringing it forward. But, straws show which way the wind blows, and we must gather these things from the material at hand. I think I am within the mark in saying that the operation of this Bill will not be such as was pictured in such a masterly way by the Minister of Finance, but that it will go much further. It is a matter which will enter much deeper into our fiscal system than the Minister of Finance would lead us to believe, if we can judge of its provisions and by the remarks which he has made to this House to-dav. I believe I am right in saying that the only occasion

on which the question was ever mentioned in this House during the past ten or twelve years, was during the last session of the last parliament, about a year ago. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) on that occasion, speaking in the debate on the question of reciprocity with the United States, did make a reference to the question of establishing a permanent tariff commission. It was not a lengthy reference, it was a brief reference and I give it now as being the only reference I can find in this House by the right hon. gentleman or by any one else to the matter. He said in that speech, at page 3311:-
I believe that we in Canada, in the future still more than in the past, should attempt to shape our tariff upon scientific consideration of known facts. I believe it would be well that we should have exact information as to these matters laid before parliament. I believe it would be well if we established a permanent tariff commission in Canada so that our tariff should not be made by rule of thumb.
And further, in column 3312, he says:
My idea of a tariff is one which would give the industries of this country a fair chaace, and more than a fair chance perhaps, to stand up against competition of countries where, it may be, the standard of living among the labouring people is lower than in Canada, and lower than it ought to be any where. That I think is a reasonable proposition. A permanent tariff commission if established would be the most fitting authority to , decide as to these points.
If that language correctly expresses what was the view and the opinion of my right hon. friend the leader of the government, when he spoke in this House one year ago, the intention of the tariff commission, and of this Bill which has been introduced, go much farther than the Minister of Finance would lead the House to believe. The right hon. leader of the government said last year that in his judgment a tariff commission would be the proper tribunal to decide these weighty matters, and he was then in favour of giving to the industries in Canada not only a fair chance, ' but more than a fair chance perhaps.' Why give to the industries of Canada more than a fair chance, let me ask my right hon. friend? Was that expression purposely used as a bait for the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and did the Canadian Manufacturers Association take the bait? Why give them more than a fair chance? Do they ask for more than a fair chance? I assume they do, but if that language correctly expresses the views of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, speaking in this House one year ago, and if this Bill is to establish a permanent tariff commission, and to give that commission power to decide these questions, as intimated by the right hon. gentleman
last year, then the Bill is not so simple, and not so innocuous as the Minister of Finance would lead the House to believe in his statement. But, Sir, I am backed up in that view by a statement which appeared a day or two ago in the columns of the ' Toronto Mail.' This is about the first serious reference I ever saw in the newspapers of Canada to the question of a permanent tariff commission. It is contained in an editorial in the ' Mail and Empire ' of February 1. It is only a passing reference, it is true, but, as I said, straws show which way the wind blows and there are one or two sentences here which indicate quite clearly that, notwithstanding the language used in the Bill, and the language used in addressing this House to-day by the Finance Minister, the real object and intent of the Bill go much farther than he would lead us to believe, and it will mean a general raising of the tariff of this country and the erection of a barrier between the people and the ministers who should be responsible to the people but who hereafter will try to shoulder that responsibility upon the board which they propose to create by this Bill. The Toronto ' Mail,' in discussing what the commission has to do, and referring to the material which the commissioners are to collect, says:
This material will not only be collected, but, which is scarcely less important, it will be organized, and something like a starting point for a scientific tariff will thus he fixed.
That so-called scientific tariff is to be organized from that starting point to b( established by these permanent tariff commissioners. Further on, in the same article, it says:
The commission's work will establish a new landmark in the history of Canadian tariff legislation.
Is that not plain enough? Do the people not believe that the government's proposal means that the board of tariff commissioners shall, from time to time, make reports upon which this government will act, and that these reports, in the very nature of things, will be in the interest of higher duties or greater protection to the industries of Canada; or, in the words of the Prime Minister, will be designed to give the industries of Canada more than a fair chance? If they give them more than a fair chance somebody is going to suffer. It is at the expense of somebody else.
At whose expense is it to be? Certainly, at the expense of the great consuming-masses of this country. I might mention one or two other matters which tend to lead me to the conclusion that we do not see the intention and the purpose of the government on the face of this Bill. It i3 only a few weeks since there appeared in the newspapers a letter from the right

hon. the Prime Minister addressed to Sir Sanford Fleming in regard to the cement merger. In that letter the right hon. gentleman said that the legal aspect of the question should be decided by the courts, and in that, I agree with him. But, he said, the question of the raising of the price by means of the merger is a matter for the Tariff Commission to deal with. It is only during the present session that I asked the Minister of Customs, on behalf of some of my constituents, whether a certain heavy triphammer could be imported from Chicago free of duty, the same not being mentioned in the Canadian Tariff and not being manufactured in Canada. I suppose my request could have been granted by order in council, but my request was refused courteously by the Minister of Customs and in his letter of refusal he said: this is another of these matters for the Tariff Commission to deal with. Now, when facts like that come to one's knowledge and when we know that the people who have established permanent Tariff Commissions throughout the world, are people who believe m the doctrine of protection to the hilt and the highest kind of protection; when we know that the only demand in Canada for a permanent Tariff Commission has been from the high protectionist party, the Canadian Manufacturers Association; when we know there has not been any earnest demand or suggestion for it from any other body of people in the Dominion, then, taking the statement of the Prime Minister, with the statement of the Minister of Customs to which I have referred and with the statement of the ' Toronto Mail and Empire ', may we not reasonably conclude that the functions of this hoard are far greater than would appear on the surface, and that the proposal is in reality a radical departure from British and from Canadian parliamentary practice?
The Bill is largely an American model, nothing more or less than a cheap Yankee device of the Finance Minister, copied from the United States; a device notoriously invented by the high protectionist party in the United States. I challenge the Minister of Finance to contradict that statement. It cannot be contradicted because it is the absolute truth. In form and in substance we have in this Bill, an American article, a cheap Yankee device, which, as one man said in Congress, was intended to sustain the glorious doctrine of protection. Coming to the Bill itself, the third clause deals with the number of commissioners, the appointment of commissioners, etc. and I notice it is not set out in that clause that these commissioners shall be possessed of any special qualifications.
I heard the Minister of Finance state in the House a few days ago, and I think Mr. GUTHRIE
quite correctly, that he would appoint no man on account of his business or calling, and that he would not refuse to appoint any man on 'account of his business or calling. But as this Bill is to create a special board for a particular purpose, I think the commissioners -to be appointed, if we go that Length, should be men having some special training or qualifications. However, no qualification at all is mentioned in the Bill, and in that respect the government will have a free hand. Now, there is one qualification that a man must have if he is to sit on that board, and that is: he must not only be a consistent supporter of the Conservative party right up to and including the last election, but he must also be a High Protectionist before he will sit on that board. The members of that hoard will be appointed from the friends of the government, 'and possibly some of the members will be recruited from the Canadian Manufacturers Association. I do not know that these people have any special qualifications to perform this class of work, but I mention this particularly because this commission is a permanent body They are not to be such a commission as the Minister of Railways had to deal with the other day when he said they were only appointed during pleasure, and he removed them. This commission once appointed cannot be removed except for cause, which means by impeachment as you would remove a judge. Once appointed they are there and they are permanently there, and the words ' for cause ' .are put in just to assure them that they are safe even if in two or three years my hon. friend the leader of the opposition should again obtain power, so that he will not be able to dismiss them. The fact, therefore, is that we are going to have three permanent tariff commissioners a board just as permanently appointed as a Bench of Judges is appointed; and that the qualification is that they shall be loyal subjects and followers of the-.-
Some lion. MEMBERS. Of the King.

Of the right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister of Canada. They are to be Conservatives first, last, and all the time, and if they aie, they have also got to be Protectionists and High Protectionists. We may make up our minds to it that we are going to have a board made up of individuals who rightly or wrongly hold opinions in favour oi a highly protective system in this Dominion.
Is not my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) a Protectionist himsellf?
I believe in a certain amount of protection; a tariff for revenue.
Tariff for tariff, the old cry.

A tariff for revenue affords enough protection in my community and in my opinion it is sufficient. Let us reason the thing out a little further. I believe that there are men in Canada, and many of them, as stated by the Minister of Finance, whose opinions are fixed on the question of Protection and High Protection. With them it is not a matter of a mere change of opinion from day to day or from year to year; they have an absolute and honest conviction that high protection-some of them would have it as high as Hainan's gallows-is the best system for Canada. I give these men credit for honestly holding these opinions. Then, there are a large number of people in this country, who believe as I believe, that if we adopt a tariff for revenue, we will have sufficient incidental protection-and some protection is necessary-for the industries of Canada. But there are also a large number of people who believe in free trade. Here we have three distinct classes of opinion on the fiscal policy of the country, and there may be more. I give these all credit for honesty of conviction, and I will ask the Prime Minister from which of these classes he proposes to appoint a permanent tariff board? I believe that_ if he appoints a board of high protectionists they will view the facts and conditions and circumstances which they are called upon to inquire into through one set of spectacles. I could name for him another set of commissioners who are just as clearly convinced that the best fecal policy for this country is free trade, and who would from the same facts the same conditions, and the sarnie surroundings, form a different conclusion altogether.
I put the matter more pointedly than that; I will put an extreme case. Take a tariff board composed of three men holding opinions such as those of my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Lalor); they would certainly be extreme protectionists. Take another board composed of three men such as my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), whom I believe to be the ablest exponent of the doctrine of free trade either in this House or in this country. I believe these two boards would view the same facts, inquire into the same conditions, and come to almost opposite conclusions upon them. Where are you going to draw the line? This Bill in my humble judgment goes much too far in the power which it gives to the commissioners. The United States Bill was more fair than this, f-or that Bill provided that the tariff boaj'd should consist of five members three of whom should be Republicans. We do not recognize the party system in our legislation, and I think it is well that we do not; but this Bill gives the government power to appoint three gentlemen of high protectionist views, and we know, without 83
going a step further, just what their view of the situation will be and what their report is likely to be. Now, the personnel and the functions of this commission are the all important things. I do not think the government should ask us to advance the Bill without giving us some information in this regard, i notice, in reading the * Congressional Record ' of the United States, that Senator La Follette said that it was absolutely essential to the consideration of the Bill that the names should be submitted; and I think it will appeal to the hon. members of this House that we ought to know something of the man whom the government intend to appoint in order that we may reach a conclusion as to their qualifications and as to whether they are men likely to perform properly the duties which this Bill proposes to assign to them. Passing on to the functions of the commission, I notice that by section 4 subsection 1 after full inquiry has been made the commissioners are required to report to the Minister of Finance. I believe it would be far more satisfactory if that were changed and the report of the commissioners were to be made directly to parliament. I see no reason whatever for limiting such a report or tying it up in the files of the Finance Department. If the information which this board obtains is of any practical value, then surely it ought to be submitted to this House in order that all hon. members would have an opportunity of perusing it. I take issue with my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in regard to the application of subsection 3 of section 4, which provides that these commissioners may inquire into combines. The Bill does not in express terms repeal the provision of the Customs Act which provides that the Governor in Council may institute proceedings before the judges of this country to inquire into combines. That provision would probably continue to be in force; but to my mind it is nothing short of ridiculous to ask a board of hidebound political commissioners to inquire into the combines and mergers dominated by their own political friends. That would be the position. Why, Sir, with a board of three Conservative commissioners of the high protectionist stripe there is not a merger or combine or trust in Canada, but would laugh in its sleeve when these gentlemen talked about having its affairs investigated. That provision in the Bill might well be removed, so that the power would remain where it now is, in the Customs Act, permitting the Governor in Council to empower the judges to make such an inquiry. 1 understand that the present Customs Act is not effective in this respect. I believe there is very much to be said in favour of the position taken by the hon. member
Hear, hear.

But it was not on the doctrine of protection, which doctrine always brings such a cheer from hon. members opposite, but on the question of reciprocal trade relations with the United States. The bulk of the farmers of Ontario are not high protectionists. And this matter will vitally affect them when brought to its logical conclusion and put in full operation. Why not let them have a fair chance to digest the Bill, to consider it? Why hurry it through? It is not going to affect the government's determination on the question of the iron and steel bounties. Because I assume that that will be announced in the near future, even before the Tariff Commission is appointed. If the leader of the government would consent to my proposal, I think it would be in the interest of everybody. If he will not consent to it, then there is nothing left for me to do on behalf of this side but to move an amendment, seconded by Mr. Pardee:
That this Bill be not now read the second time, but that it be read the second time this day six months.

speechtext:
I took down his words.
I withdraw the meaning which I would have otherwise attributed to them, if he tells me that he did not intend to convey that meaning. But he certainly did, in the latter part of his speech, use words which conveyed that impression to my mind, because I took them down. He said:
The result of this would be a tariff brought in by an irresponsible Tariff Commission.
That is what he said, I do not know what he meant. If he did not mean that, I accept at once his disclaimer; it is my duty under the rules of parliament to do so. This Tariff Commission will bring in no tariff; the government of this country wij.l bring in the tariff, in the future as in the. past. To contrast the two methods, I myself remember what took place in this Houise in 1897, and more especially in 1907. When the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Trade and Commerce had .ionrneyed around this country, had listened to speeches here and there, from this man, and that man, and the other man, in every city and every important town in Canada, they came back to parliament and brought down a tariff, and I ask what information was available to any man in this House from all the peregrinations and pilgrimages of these three gentle men? I asked that the result of their labours should be brought down, and they brought down, in typewritten form, not even printed and indexed, and piled up on the table of this House a mass of papers two or three .feet in height, and I do not think any member of this House ever took the time, or pains, or trouble to pay the slightest attention to it, from beginning to end of the debate. My hon. friend may have been an exception, I do not know whether he was or not; I know that he is very industrious in sudh matters. Now, what we propose is to have a Tariff Commission of mien who will be wisely selected for that purpose, and who will collect information in a systematic and effective manner, and put it in such a form that the government can avail themselves of it; information which will he available for the purpose of discussion in this parliament when any tariff changes are proposed. Surely there is no radical departure in all that. My hon. friend repeated over and
over again that this is a radical departure, that this would create a barrier. Let us take his own illustration. He says the same result could be arrived at if the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Customs would add certain officers to their staffs	and	acquire
information in that way. May I be permitted to inquire of the thoughtful members of this House who listened to my hon. friend, why the obtaining of information in the one way would create a barrier and would not create a barrier in the other way. Has a single hon. gentleman in this House been able to compass the argument of my hon. friend in that respect? I do not think he has been able to compass it himself; at all events, he will have an opportunity, I hope of telling us on some later occasion, just what he meant by that extraordinary argument and still more extraordinary suggestion. Then he is very much disturbed as to some of the provisions of this Bill, he was very much disturbed as to the provision that evidence not taken under oath may be used. Does he not remember that about ten days ago lie and a number of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House were very much disturbed because a commission was to be appointed who would take evidence on oath? At that time the great danger was that commissioners should be appointed to take evidence on oath, and now he Is greatly disturbed because commissioners are to be appointed who may take evidence not under oath.
I did not take any exception as to the question of oath, it was the kind of evidence I objected to, it was to be too wide.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I thought my hon. friend was alluding to that clause in the Bill which says:-
For the purpose of any inquiry under this \ct the commissioners may obtain information which in their judgment i9 authentic, otherwise than under the sanction of an oath or affirmation, and use and act upon such information.
I may have misunderstood my hon. friend, I am sorry if I did so. But I understood that the objection he raised to that section was that evidence not taken under the sanction of an oath, might be used by the commission. Was not that the objection which he raised?

What I meant to say, was that material which was really not evidence at all, might be used if the commissioners saw fit; letters, conversations, or anything of that kind. The objection was not to the lack of an oath.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, then I do not understand my hon. friend's objection at all.

I would not suppose that a commission of this kind would he bound by formal rules of evidence; at all events, I would hope that they would not make any attempt to restrict their inquiry by rules of that kind. Therefore it seems to me my hon. friend's objection falls to the ground.
Now, my hon. friend was very much concerned about the attitude of the government towards the Manufacturers' Association. I want to tell my hon. friend that he ought not to assume too much in these matters without due inquiry. So far as I am concerned, no man connected with the Manufacturers' Association of Canada ever spoke to me on this subject, except one, and he was absolutely opposed to the establishment of a permanent tariff commission. I want to tell my hon. friend, further, that no promise has ever been made by this government to the Manufacturers' Association; and further than that, the Manufacturers' Association have never approached the government for the purpose of obtaining any promise.	.
My hon. friend must not draw too much upon his own experience or the experience of his party friends in that regard. That -is not the way in which the present administration propose to conduct the affairs of this country-by making promises of modifying the tariff in consideration of political support at elections. We have put all that behind us; the country put such methods behind it at the last election. My hon. friend finds fault with us for establishing this Tariff Commission, because he says that a commission of this character is only to be found in countries that have established a highly protective system. Again, I do not know that my hon. friend has been exceedingly accurate. It is perfectly true that a commission, or something of that kind, exists in France, and it may exist in Germany, although I am not sure of that. A Bill has been introduced into the Congress of the United States, but, if I understand the situation correctly, it has not yet been passed. It has not been passed for the reason that very grave objection, I believe, has been raised to it there. So, if my hon. friend regards the United States as a highly protectionist country, let me point out to him the simple fact that this Bill, up to the present time, has failed to pass the Congress of the United States. Further than that, I think that the object of the President of the United States in introducing that Bill, and in defending the establishment of a permanent Tariff Commission in that country was to cut down the system of protection in order that it might be brought within reasonable bounds. Surely my hon. friend is aware that at the last Imperial Conference held within a year his own leader stood up before that conference and moved I

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
for an Imperial Trade Commission to investigate conditions of trade in every one of the great Dominions which owe allegiance to His Majesty the King. I suppose the idea in making that proposal was to establish a means by which the necessary information as to trade conditions in every one of these Dominions, both within themselves and in relation to the people of the mother country, could be gathered in an effective way. If the proposal made on that occasion was a good one, why is it after all that my hon. friend finds any fault with the proposal of the present administration to do in an effective, systematic and thorough way that which in the past has been done in a very differenl manner?
I do not know that there is very much else in w'hat my hon. friend has suggested to which attention need be given at the present time. As far a.s the provisions of the Customs Act are concerned, to which my hon. friend has alluded, the only thing that this Bill accomplishes, if it should pass into law, is this, that it establishes another tribunal to which may be referred the question as to whether or not a particular combine does' or does not exist in this country. It does not take away any existing powers. It simply adds a new tribunal and in that regard surely it is a step in the right direction.
When my hon. friend suggested to us that we should have officers appointed for the purpose of enforcing Dominion legislation, I think he possibly made the most sensible suggestion that I noticed in his speech. But, I am bound to say that, although it has been spoken of in this parliament for the past six or seven years and advocated by my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) and other hon members of the House, I do not think that suggestion, up to the present time, has received any sympathy or support from the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat and I am glad to observe the newly awakened interest in the enforcement of Federal laws which has just been- developed by my hon. friend. This is a matter to which we intend to give very serious consideration. It is impossible to deal with all these matters at once. As far as my views are concerned, I think there is a great deal in the suggestions which have been made for many" years past by my hon. friend from South York and by other hon. members of this House in line with what has been suggested by my hon. friend from South Wellington.
My hon. friend has screwed his courage to the sticking point and has proposed an amendment. He has proposed an amendment that this- Bill shall not be read now, but that it shall be read this day six months hence. We are glad to

welcome the challenge that my hon. friend has thrown out. He was very insinuating in his suggestion at first that we should have regard to the interests of the people and withdraw this Bill, but, at the end, he made manifest his true intention which was to challenge the policy of the government in this regard and to propose a continuance of the old method pursued in 1897 and in 1907 of conducting by useless and ineffective methods any investigations into the trade conditions of the country, the cost of production and all those matters that are so important to a proper consideration of this question. We believe that this information is necessary, that it ought to be obtained in a systematic and businesslike way and that it cannot be so obtained by the old methods. We propose now a method which takes away from parliament absolutely nothing of that power which is vested in parliament and of which parliament cannot divest itself. We propose to take away nothing of that, but we do propose to appoint a Tariff Commission which will give to the government and to parliament information respecting all matters that have been alluded to which information is vital, essential and necessary in order that a reasonable and just tariff may be made in . the interest of the people of this country. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I do trust that the hon. members of this House will not regard with favour the proposal of my hon. friend to defer this legislation to another session. I trust that the amendment made be defeated and, that this Bill may be passed. So far as the appointments are concerned, I can only say to my hon. friend from South Wellington that we do not know at the present time whom we shall appoint to that commission, but when we do make the appointments we believe they will be such as will commend themselves not only to the judgment of this House, but to the judgment of the country as well. I therefore, say, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, that the government cannot for one moment think of accepting the proposal of my hon. friend from South Wellington and that we desire to have this legislation passed and passed at this session. We do not desire to limit in any way the discussion upon the question but we believe that it is in the interest of parliament and of the people of the country that the Bill should become law at the earliest possible opportunity. The right hon. .gentleman the Prime Minister complained that the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), did noit discuss the principles of the Bill Ibefore the House, but the right hon. gentleman himself did not come within many degrees of latitude and longitude of discussing any single principle involved in the Bill, and it would have been more illuminating to the House had he scolded less and argued more. He referred to the attitude of the hon. member (Mr. Guthrie) upon the reciprocal trade arrangement with the United States in a scolding fashion, but what that had to do with the Bill we were discussing is more than I can understand. If the right hon. gentleman does himself understand the principles -involved in the Bill, then he was most successful in neglecting to disclose his knowledge to the House. The hon. member from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), was distinctly right when he said that this measure was a mere copy of Yankee legislation which has not yet even received the approval of the American Gongress. There is no originality in the Bill, and, apparently on the part of the ministers there is no attempt to understand what principle underlies it, if principle there be. The right hon. gentleman complained that the hon. member (Mr. Guthrie) objected to the appointment of a Tariff Commission as provided for in this Bill, while, at the same time, he formally admitted the feasibility and propriety of the addition to the Civil Service of a certain staff in order to enable members of the government to prepare a tariff. Well, if the right hon. gentleman failed to understand the distinction between the two, he has ' failed to understand what the Bill involves. I am opposed to his Bill, because I believe it is a violation of constitutional practice in all British countries, because it directly or indirectly, and perhaps unconsciously, assumes to give to a Tariff Commission powers of legislation
How?

I will tell you how later. I object to it because it tends to weaken the doctrine of ministerial responsibility as it obtains in all British countries; I object to it because the duties which, under the Bill, are assigned to a commission, refer to matters which in all British countries, are dealt with directly by the responsible advisers of the Crown. I object to the Bill, because the purpose sought to be attained by it can be better attained by less expensive and less objectionable methods; I object to it further, because it seeks in a manner-in a veiled manner, perhaps-to validate by a statute the doctrine of protection in this country. Recently the Minister of Finance stated in

the House that this measure was submitted in consequence of the popular demand. I deny that. It is true that the creation of a Tariff Commission has been suggested by the Manufacturers' Association, and by certain other individuals, and at is true that the Prime Minister, during the recent election campaign, did occasionally refer to the appointment of a permanent Tariff Commission, but not in a very serious manner, because I do not remember a single occasion upon which he devoted more than a few minutes to that particular matter. I submit that there is no evidence whatever of any demand by the people of this country for the appointment of such a commission. The establishment of this commission does not meet with the approval of the matured thought of this country, and from personal experience I know that it does not meet- with favour from a great many who live within protectionist circles. I think it may be safely said that the government adopted this idea of a Tariff Commission merely as an expedient to escape a frank declaration of their policy upon trade and tariff matters during the past few months. It was, in the first instance, compounded as a sedative for the people of western Canada, who were demanding wider markets and reciprocal trade with the United States. It is an artificial expedient to escape ministerial responsibility, and its effect will be to further becloud an already difficult problem. When we read the declaration of the Prime Minister, in what is known as his Halifax platform, on the fiscal policy of the country, one would imagine that no other human agency than the government itself was necessary to frame a tariff that would suit all sections of the country, and all classes of people. I shall read the tariff plank from the Halifax platform, and it will then be seen that in some respects it might be properly catalogued as humorous, although it was delivered in the most solemn manner. I might also add that in some respects it is like the Divine peace, which ' passeth all understanding.' It reads:
'Fiscal policy which will promote the production within Canada of all useful articles and commodities that can be advantageously produced or manufactured from or by means of our natural resources, having due regard to the interests of the consumer, as well as to the just claims of our wage-earning population.'
Hear, hear.

I am glad to hear hon. gentlemen opposite express approval of the declaration of their leader, but if they had faith in the ability of their leader to carry out their trade policy as thus announced, there would be no necessity for this tariff board. When one thinks Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
of the difficulty in framing a tariff in this country that will suit the producer, the consumer, and the wage-earner and remembers that the Prime Minister stated, in announcing his tariff policy, that he and his party could accomplish this difficult task, it is strange that he and his party, having the open sesame to tariff-making on the universally harmonious plan, should seek the intervention of a Tariff Commission or any other body. In his Halifax platform the right hon. gentleman stated that it was his policy, in framing a tariff, to protect the producer, to protect the consumer and to protect the labourer as well, a task which passes the power of any man on earth. Was this declaration of policy on the part of the Prime Minister a wilful deception, or has the boastfulness which characterized hon. gentlemen opposite in the days when they were in opposition been tempered somewhat by the responsibilities of office? Now, the Bill before the House seeks to establish a Tariff Commission to which are as-signed_ certain duties, which are directly or indirectly related to tariff-making. I do not propose to discuss the various clauses of the Bill, as they have already been fully and fairly dealt with by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). I desire merely to discuss the principle involved in the Bill, namely, the appointment of a commission to assist in the matter of taxation by tariffs and tariffs for protection.

House resumed at eight o'clock.

Before recess I was laying down the proposition that there was a principle involved in this Bill. I was submitting that the appointment of this Tariff Commission involved a departure from a well established principle in our constitution and in this respect differs from the appointment of any other commission. The right hon. the First Minister this afternoon argued that as parliament had appointed in the past many other commissions and no objection was raised, there should be no objection to the appointment of a Tariff Commission. If the right hon. gentleman is really of the opinion that this Tariff Commission differs in no essential from others, I can quite understand why he should treat the whole subject so cavalierly. But if there be a distinction between the proposed Tariff Commission and other commissions, I cannot understand the position taken by my right hon. friend. I would ask the government, why in this particular instance, it has departed from the customary practice of administering public affairs

through the civil service under responsible ministers. Why. in the matter of taxation and revenue, interject between the people and the government, between the legislative and executive powers of this parliament, a new body to be called the Tariff Commission? If the Depaitment of Finance is in need of additional expert aid for the transaction of the business of that department, no hon. member of this House will object to any money vote which will give that department the number of competent men required to carry on its business. That would be a much better method than the one proposed, because it would ensure permanency, for, of course, the appointments to the civil service are much more permanent than the appointments of commissioners. Why single out a number of gentlemen as members of this Tariff Commission and give each a salary almost equal to that of a minister, for the performance of duties which can be performed just as well and possibly better by clerks in the civil service? So far as I am concerned, I would willingly vote for the appointment of such extra officials in the Departments of Finance, Trade and Commerce and Customs as would give the minister in each of these departments an efficient staff upon which he could rely, especially in matters connected with the tariff. That has been my view for years, and while I may not have given public utterance to it, I have expressed it to some members of the late government, political friends of my own. If that were done, we would have a civil service staff working under the direction of the minister of the day, no matter to what political party he might belong. The framing of a tariff for Canada is a matter of policy which, under constitutional and parliamentary practice, rests with the government. No money or taxation measure -and the tariff is eminently such a measure-can originate with parliament or any member of it. The government may accept a suggestion from parliament or from any member of parliament, but in acting on that suggestion it does so solely on its own responsibility, because it is the government of the day which is primarily responsible in matters of taxation. Not even the Senate can interfere in such matters. The isolation of the government in this respect, its undivided responsibility, is well illustrated by the fact that when the Finance Minister brings down a tariff Bill the moment he submits to parliament the first item of that tariff, the whole Bill goes into effect from coast to coast. Therefore, the responsible minister in these matters-the Finance Minister -should not ask for the passage of a
statute that will create a body to deal with the tariff and thus divide his responsibility. When he does so, he is violating the constitutional practice of this country. Again a Tariff Commission is entitled to no more consideration than parliament or any one member of parliament, yet should this Bill go into effect and this Tariff Commission be created, the members of that commission will, in the making of tariffs, have more to say than any member of parliament. In case it be argued that the distinction I make between assistance given to the Finance Minister by a Tariff Commission and that given to him by a staff in the civil service, is a very fine distinction, let me point out that to any one who keep in view the constitutional principle, and the constitutional practice of this country, the distinction will be obvious. In this connection it may not perhaps be amiss for me to give the view to be found in Bourinot's ' Parliamentary Procedure ' regarding the imposition of taxation. These will be found on page 594:
It is now a fixed principle of constitutional government that all propositions for the imposition of taxes should emanate from the minister. In the session of 1871 Mr. Speaker Coekburn recommended to the House the adoption of the British practice in this particular, and the Commons have ever since acquiesced in its wisdom. As a consequence no private member is now permitted to propose a Dominion tax upon the people; it must proceed from a minister of the Crown, or be in some other form declared to he necessary for the public service. A motion or a Bill of such a character should properly be introduced by a minister of the Crown.
Now, the Minister of Finance in proposing the appointment of a Tariff Commission, is dividing the responsibility which constitutional parliamentary practice has thrown on him in this respect.
Therefore, I venture to postulate the statement that no member of parliament originates a tariff or taxation Bill. He has the power to recommend changes, but, before it can become effective, it must be recognized by the ministry of the day, and, in the last analysis, by the Minister of Finance. The Tariff Commission to be appointed under this Bill will be given power to investigate facts and report. It is to be appointed, apparently, upon the assumption that taxation by tariffs with the feature of protection, is constitutional in this country. If the Bill means anything, it means that the principle of protection-and I am not arguing against it now-is constitutional in this country, or we seek to make it so by placing that principle in a statute. It is placed in such a position that if any of the members of the commission have views upon the tariff, they can practically compel recognition of them by parliament. And

this is only natural because the Bill by which it is proposed to appoint this commission practically places the members ot the commission on a parity or at least in partnership with the Minister of Finance. And I say the commission in this respect is given a prominence which the constitution of this country never contemplated, and our parliamentary practice does not warrant. The members of the commission are given a rank above the members of parliament.
It has been urged, and it will be urged again, that because there was created in the United States a so called tariff board, that conditions are analogous in both countries, and hon. gentlemen opposite will urge, as I think the Minister of Finance did, that because the United States appointed a tariff board or commission, therefore, this parliament should appoint one. Let us review what has been done in the United States in this respect, and let us see if the methods of tariff making in Canada and the United States are analogous; let us inquire if, even though there were, in the United States a Tariff Commission or a tariff board, we should be warranted in appointing one in Canada. In the United States there is no such thing as a Tariff Commission, and there may never be *-likely there never will be. Strictly speaking, there i3 no tariff board. In the United States tariff of 1909 there appeared for the first time the principle of a maximum and a minimum tariff, and section 2 of that Tariff Act places upon the President the authority to determine against which countries, if any, the maximum and the minimum tariffs should apply, and when the maximum tariff, if applied, shall be withdrawn. The same Tariff Bill provided by a money vote the means by which the President could secure such information as would be necessary to determine when he should apply the maximum tariff against any country, and when he should withdraw it. Now that is all there is in the nature of tariff board or tariff commission legislation in the United States; and, strictly speaking I say there is not even a tariff board in that country. There is only given the power under the annual Appropriation Act, to the president to employ the services of any persons whom he may select to assist him in determining when and against which countries he shall apply the maximum or the minimum tariff.
If that be so, how is it that the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) accused the Minister of Finance of following ' cheap Yankee methods '?
I can see a very clear and obvious distinction. I can also quite understand and justify the statement that the hon. member for South Wel-

In the United States there is no such thing as a civil service so far as tariff making is concerned, and even the President of the United States, while having [lower to recommend changes in the tariff, is absolutely powerless to initiate any such change.
No such body exists in the United States, and the effort promptly to put the question of revision on a sound basis, therefore, involves a much more extensive labour of investigation than would otherwise be necessary.
Now, you have only to look at the tariff of the United States to see its obvious defects as to classification and rates. The Canadian tariff, as far as classification is concerned, is fairly suitable, although open to improvement, and while the protective principle obtains in this country, it can be safely said that neither party has gone protection mad, as in the case of the United States, and, therefore, in tariff revision, and tariff making, we are not in the same position as they are. 1 suggest to the Finance Minister, as I suggested three years ago to Mr. Fielding, when Minister of Finance, that there should be a branch of the civil service to assist the Minis-of Finance in tariff making. I say that would be better than the appointment of a Tariff Commission. The Departments of Finance, of Trade and Commerce, and of Customs, are closely connected w'ith the matter of tariff making, and I would suggest, as an alternative to this Tariff Commission, the selection of

proper officials from these three departments, organizing them if you will, under the name of a tariff bureau, and adding to their duties, if you feel so disposed, the obtaining of trade statistics which is very much needed in this country. The advantage of this would be that the members of this staff or bureau would be members of the civil service; they would be permanently in office, they would be unknown to the public other than civil servants, and according to the true constitutional practice, the minister alone would be responsible to parliament. I suppose it is fair to assume that directly or indirectly protection obtains in the tariffs of this country. It has been said by some, and indeed by no less a person that the Prime Minister himself, that a tariff can be scientifically framed by a Tariff Commission, and that this Tariff Commission would take the tariff out of politics. But, I was pleased to hear the Minister of Finance say to-day that there was no such thing as taking the tariff out of polities, and that it was impossible to give a scientific tariff. It is beyond human ingenuity for a Tariff Commission, or for any other body, to draft a Tariff Bill covering whole ranges of industry, which will be free of all inequalities and anomalies. Such a thing as scientific tariff making, where the protective principle is present, is an absolute absurdity. I am surprised that any hon. member of this House, especially the right hon. the Prime Minister, should believe that such a thing as scientific tariff making is possible.
To determine with scientific accuracy what is raw product, is an impossibility in a tariff in which the protective feature obtains. In Canadian trade the manufactured product of one industry is the raw material of another. The man who weaves the yarn does not spin it; the tailor begins with cloth, but does not make it, the shoemaker begins with manufactured leather, but rarely, if ever, makes it; the foun-dryman who uses pig-iron does not make pig-iron; the automobile manufacturer uses a great variety of materials, but manufactures practically nothing among all the articles which when -assembled constitute an automobile. When hon. gentlemen talk about a scientific tariff, they are attaching to the word ' scientific ' an improper meaning, because science loves truth, and the word ' scientific ' in this -case is not a token of that which is true. In the last analysis protective tariffs are not determined with scientific accuracy; it is impossible that they can be. The question of tariffs, protective tariffs, is largely a ' case of might. Local considerations, and the weight of influence brought by -sections of the country and by various classes of pro-Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
ducers are always more apparent in tariffmaking than the influence of scientific or economic truths. At the best tariff-making is but rough approximations. From the protective standpoint the test is. the force of foreign competition in the domestic market; and when you once ascertain the selling price of a foreign article in the coan-try of production and the price of the same article in the Canadian market, that is, cost, insurance and freight, you have substantially the crux of the wliole question. . These facts are obtainable without difficulty and without an expensive instrument like a formal commission. They can be obtained as readily by the Minister of Finance with an efficient civil service staff as by any tariff board. Again, everybody knows that there are so many conflicting and fluctuating conditions in trade that it is impossible to draw any conclusion from the facts obtained one year which would be helpful to a minister framing a tariff containing the principle of protection, the following year. In framing a. revenue tariff you need no experts and no tariff commission. In one country in certain trades the hours of labour are longer than in others. In our country you will find one manufacturer so efficient that he can get along without a tariff, while perhaps right alongside of him is another producer so inefficient in his methods that no amount of protection could make an intelligent or profitable producer of him. Then you have changing transportation rates, changing transportation routes, wars and rumours of wars, monetary and business crises, changes of foreign tariffs, changes in rates of interest, the effect of climatic changes, all to consider; and all these conditions would in a short time render futile any investigation of facts produced at the cost of a great expenditure of time, of work and of money by any commission. After all, the reports of such a commission cannot be more than rough approximations, which could be obtained just as well by other methods. I have already said that the appointment of a tariff commission by parliament is a statutory and legal recognition of the protective theory, and whether we are free traders, revenue tariff men or protectionists, we should not enact any statute implying that that principle should obtain in our tariff; but that is the effect of the appointment of a tariff commission by statute. During the discussion of the Tariff Board Bill in the United States Congress, one member of the House of Representatives said that he supported the Bill because it contained the principles of the bulwark of protection, and I am sure that a great -many of the hon. gentlemen opposite are going to support this Bill because they feel that the Tariff Commission will be the bulwark of protection in this
