country. Another gentleman in the United States House of Representatives said that if he believed in only a revenue tariff he would not support the Tariff Board Bill. The present Prime Minister, during the last election campaign, strongly declared himself on several occasions in favour of protection, and followed with the statement that the late government had revised the tariff without ascertaining all the conditions surrounding the tariff, and that when his party came into power he would appoint a commission to revise the tariff along business lines. Now, I submit that these several statements of the Prime Minister taken together can only mean that the right hon. gentleman believed that the commission to be created would assist in giving the protective feature to the tariff of this country. They could mean nothing else. I do not imagine that he would complain that the late government had increased the tariff in any respect. I assume that if he was complaining of anything, it was of reductions in the tariff which he said were made without proper ascertainment of the facts. Now, I do not say that I object to a tariff, even a protective tariff. I am not arguing one way or the other; but I do say that if we are going to have a tariff with the protective feature in this country, let parliament say so.
Every member of parliament should at least have as much to say regarding that as the members of a Tariff Commission. The Minister of Finance this afternoon sought to buttress his argument in favour of the commission by saying that we received $74,000,000 of our revenue from customs. No doubt he wanted us to draw the conclusion that a Tariff Commis-mission was justifiable because so much of our revenue came from the tariff. Much of our customs revenue comes from imported articles, the duties on which are intended to protect, but protected items give the minimum of revenue, otherwise the duties would not be protective. Therefore, the commission will- not have much to do with items bearing only revenue rates, and from the standpoint of revenue they will not have much to do with protected items, because these items are not great revenue producers. It is not intended that they should have much to do with the matter of revenue, but that their work would be devoted mainly to the making of tariffs containing the principle of protection. Protection would, therefore, be the main reason for the existence of this commission. I do not see how any other conclusion can be drawn. In all matters respecting tariff taxation, divergent views obtain, and if we are going to apply the protective theory, it ought to be applied solely on the responsibility of the government and the minister in charge of the
Finance Department. If protection be then applied, we can take it as the expression of the wishes of the people through their responsible ministers. That tariff may have inaccuracies and inequalities, but these would be the fault of the system, and for them the government wou'ld be responsible. That method would be true to constitutional practice.
Again it may be urged that the appointment of a Tariff Commission cannot be distinguished from commissions already appointed. That was argued by the right hon. the First Minister this afternoon. In fact that was the only answer he gave to the speech of my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). In, the first place let me say that this parliament has never delegated to any commission the power of directing taxation. I know of no instance in the history of the country when that was done. We have appointed commissions to execute the will of parliament expressed regarding any undertaking, such as the National Transcontinental railway. Before the Transcontinental Commission was appointed, parliament had expressed its policy, and the commission was only appointed to carry out that policy. Reference was made this afternoon to the Railway Commission, but that is not analogous to the Tariff Commission. The Railway Commission is a court, appointed under the Railway Act. Parliament defined the jurisdiction and powers of that commission, and settled its duties and powers before making the appointment. We have appointed commissions in the past and no doubt will appoint others in the future, but it is not the practice in any British country to appoint a commission for the purpose of determining a policy or a principle. In that irespect the Tariff Commission differs from any other we have ever had. I would refer hon. gentlemen to Todd, the well known authority on parliamentary procedure. On page 432 of Todds ' Parliamentary Procedure,' I find the following:
Preliminary inquiries- by a royal commission are of inestimable service to the working of parliamentary government. Besides peculiar facilities for ascertaining facts, they
oquently bring to light a mass of information upon the subject in hand which could be obtained in no other way, and the report of an able and impartial commission is often of the highest value in the instruction and enlightenment of the public mind. The questions of pauperism and poor law administration, of crime and penal administration, of pestilence and sanitary legislation, and of the evils attendant on excessive manufacturing labour, are conspicuous instances of the effects of commissions of inquiry in reversing every main principle, and almost every assumed chief elementary fact, on which the general public, parliamentary . committees,

and leading statesmen, were prepared to legislate.
Again on page 434 Todd says:
Since the establishment of ministerial responsibility, commissions have become a recognized part of our governmental machinery, and it is now freely admitted that when confined to matters of legitimate inquiry they serve a most useful and beneficial purpose.
To all of which I agree. Every one will agree with this. It is proven by the fact that in the past parliament has unanimously concurred in the appointment of commissions for several purposes. But there is a qualification. On pages 434, and 435, Todd says:
But it would be unconstitutional to refer to a royal commisson ' subjects which are connected with the elementary duties of the executive government and with its relations to parliament '; or, to investigate a grievance which arises out of a particular decision of parliament, on a given question; or, to appoint a commission with a view to evade the responsibility of ministers in any matter; or, to do the wort of existing departments of state, which possess all needful facilities for obtaining information upon questions of detail, and which are directly responsible to parliament.
Then on page 435 I find the following:
A commission of inquiry should be limited in its operations to obtaining information, and suggesting the points to which it might be expedient that legislative or executive action should be directed. No commission should be invited to ' enter upon any question of policy/ lest it should trench upon the proper limits of ministerial responsibility, and upon ground which belongs to parliament.
I say it is a weakness of the Tariff Bill now before the House that it trenches upon the proper limit of ministerial responsibility and upon gounds which belong entirely to parliament.
There are one or two instances in the parliamentary experience of England to which I wish to refer very briefly. In 1865 Mr. Roebuck, a member of the British House of Commons, asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer if it was the intention of the government to institute an inquiry into the English railway system with a view to future legislation should such legislation appear practicable and advantageous. I cannot give to the House in full the statement made by the Chancellor, but I will endeavour to give a few quotations in order to fortify the position I have taken:
It is not their intention to take any step which could under any circumstances at all compromise or commit either ourselves or parliament with reference to any legislation upon a matter of this vast importance. . . .
Therefore, I beg that it may be understood that it is not the intention of Her Majesty's Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
government to adivise the appointment of any commission that shall enter upon any nuestion of policy. We are of opinion that if we were to doso we should be, if not prejudging the opinion of parliament, in some degree by extraneous instruments trespassing upon ground which belongs to parliament. . . We, of course, have taken into our consideration the question whether it would be desirable that this inquiry should be conducted by a Royal Commission or by a committee of this House. If we were going to inquire into any matter of policy it would, undoubtedly, be far more useful to institute that inquiry by means of a committee of this House than by means of a commission.
Again, it was once moved in the English House of Commons that an address be presented to Her Majesty that she would be graciously pleased to issue a Royal Commission directing investigation of the causes which led to the late severe and protracted pressure in the money market. Speaking to that motion Sir Stafford Northcote expressed the principle in opposition to the appointment of a commission which I have urged in connection with the tariff commission. He. said in referring to the member who had moved the resolution:
I am bound to ask the bou. member for Stockport what exactly are the functions which he thinks this Royal Commission of inquiry should undertake. Is it to he a commission which is to inquire into facts, or is it to be a commission which is to inquire into principles? I think he will see that there is very great difference between file two. If we are to investigate a number of facts, requiring a great amount of time to ascertain and bring together, undoubtedly a Royal Commission may be, and very often is, a very convenient instrument for the purpose; but if we are to discuss principles, and if we are to investigate the principles upon which our legislation is founded, I do not myself think that a Royal Commission ought to be considered a proper substitute either for the action of the government or for that of parliament. If you were to appoint a Royal Commission in this case, for the purpose of investigating all the principles of legislation which affect our currency and banking, the first question that would arise would be, bow is that commission to be constituted? We know perfectly well that different opinions prevail, and are ably maintained by the different schools of opinion, on all the questions that bear upon this subject; and if a Royal Commission were to be appointed it would be necessary to place upon that commission men in whose skill and intelligence, and in whose experience also, the country would have confidence . . . We also know that when it should become our duty to make a selection of the gentlemen-few in number as they necessarily would be-to be placed in that important position, we could not select gentlemen who a cre merely known to be gentlemen of intelligence and experience, but we should have to select gentlemen whose views upon these questions were perfectly well known and

familiar to fclie world, and probably it would not be very difficult, as soon as tbey were named, and the object of the commission made public, to foresee what the general verdict of the commission would be upon some of the main principles which would have to be brought before it. _ If that were the case, at once the authority of a commission, and therefore the use of a commission as far as the investigation of principles is concerned, would be at an end. Those who were satisfied with the opinions of the gentlemen who might be the majority in the commission would, of course, anticipate the proceedings, and foresee that their opinions would be well brought forward, well argued, and very ably, no doubt, elaborated; while on the other hand, the minority, who would not be satisfied would say, ' Because you have constituted the commission on this or the other basis, you have failed to obtain a fair verdict. We dispute, and have always disputed, the doctrines of those gentlemen forming the majority of the commission, and we also dispute the conclusion at which they have arrived.' This being the case we should not be much forwarder when we got the report of the Royal Commission than we are at the present time. . . .
And again:
It is obvious, however, that when you come to investigate causes it is not sufficient merely to collect facts, but to collect them with a view to certain conclusions, and select them upon some kind of principles. When you investigate facts, the question of causes necessarily arises.
Now, I submit that the purpose and object of a Tariff Commission finds no analogy in our political history. We have never, so far as I can ascertain, appointed a commission to determine principles of trade, tariff and taxation, upon which, in all countries of the world and in all ages divergent views do and will obtain. Let us adhere to constitutional practice. It is no answer to say that the commission is granted no legislative power; it will unconsciously and indirectly legislate. I say that in one form or another the commission will legislate or cause parliament to legislate in the direction of the conclusions and upon the facts which they present to the ministers. They are given power to supply facts, to report conclusions upon the propriety and extent of a tariff which contains the protective features. I cannot see how hon. gentlemen opposite can deny that this is the object of the Tariff Commission. If this be not the object, I say the Tariff Commission has no duty to perform. They would not be asked to investigate facts ands report upon them if free trade obtained in this country or if our tariff were based upon revenue needs. I say. this is a question of policy, and, therefore, let the people,, through a lvspmtsabV minister make the .tariff; do not let a	commission
appointed	by parliament	make it.
The manufacturers of pig iron, according to the press, are to receive a bounty pending a report from the Tariff Commission. I do not know whether that is true or not, nor am I saying whether I am for or against a bounty on pig iron, but even before the creation of the commission, according to this report we find the government absolving itself of its functions -and delegating them to >a commission yet to be appointed. That is clear and forcible evidence of the influence which the commission will exercise, and it is that influence to which I object. To-day, we find that the government cannot wait for the Tariff Commission; they are going to forestall the commission.
They are going to give advantage to a certain industry, which may be right or may be wrong, without waiting for this great power which we are seeking to create to-night. I suppose that to-morrow, or in the near future, we will hear the government saying to other interests Which will appear before them asking for higher tariffs, that they cannot 'act until they hear from the Tariff Commission; and soon it will come that you cannot tell who in this country will be making tariffs, the government or the commission, it will be absolutely impossible to tell. They will be on a parity, or they will be in partnership. I am sure that this country would prefer that we remain true to the consti-utional practice and parliamentary procedure of the past, and have no special body who will stand between the government and parliament in the making of tariffs.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to the Bill because the creation of a Tariff Commission with power to investigate and report, must ultimately mean the assumption, partially or wholly, of the power of tariff making by such a commission, or at least we will find a division of responsibility between the commission and the government. I object to this Bill because it is a subversion of the well established principle of ministerial responsibility so long obtaining in this country, particularly in reference to the question of taxation and of revenue. I object to this Bill because it purports to lend and does lend parliamentary sanction to the economic doctrine of protection. I object to it because the proposed eommipsion cannot accomplish what is expected of it in the direction of scientific tariff making. I object to it because the tariff commission cannot take the tariff out of politics, it will put it further into politics. I object to it because any merits which the Tariff Commis-, sion Bill possesses, and upon its face it does possess starve, are obtainable by the ordinary methods ji<>w, employed in the administration of the public service by



the civil service under ministerial responsibility. We may have protection in the tariff of this country to-day, we may have it in the future. I am not now arguing for or against the protective feature in our tariff; but I do say that if it is to be found in our tariff, it is better that a responsible minister and a responsible ministry place it there, and that subsequently, if the people of this country wish it to become law, it be affirmed by the parliament of this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. B. AMES (St. Antoine, Montreal).
speechtext:
We have listened, Mr. Speaker, for upwards of two hours to one of the best exemplifications I think I have ever seen since I entered this House, of the good old fable of the wolf and the lamb. After endeavouring to criticise everything that was not in the Bill, the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has finally ended by saying that if all these things that he criticises were not there, he could still read into the Bill sinister intentions, and that these sinister intentions alone were reason enough why the Bill should be rejected. Now, I propose to take half an hour in dealing with what is in the Bill. In the first place, let me say that I think if there is anything that has been demonstrated beyond per-adventure in the recent general elections, it- is that the majority of the people of Canada to-day are still believers in the National Policy that has been in force for many years. The majority of the people to-day, within reasonable limits, are willing that there should be built up and established throughout Canada diversified industries that will give employment to our people; and they .are willing, even at the risk of a slight increase of price to the consumer in some instances, that there should be a moderate protective tariff. Now, the tariff we have to-day is partially- protective and partially non-pro tective. Hitherto we have made our tariffs in a rough and ready sort of way, by rule of thumb, so to speak, and if one looks down the category of the various items he will see that it is very much like a wavy line. I wras pleased to hear the admission from the junior member for Halifax, of the fact that his experience for the last few years has gone to prove that it was ' might ' that made the tariff. That that admission should be made by one who was so close to the late government, certainly shows what has been their experience in connection therewith. I think if there is anything that this Bill proposes to do, it is to reduce at least to a minimum, the influence of 'might' in the making of tariffs1. Now, if one glances at the tariff of to-day he will find it is like a wavy line swerving first to one side and then to the other. It shows all through the Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
evidence of pressure on the part, let us say, of certain favoured producers, and then it shows the evidence of pressure in another direction on the part of certain clamorous consumers, who have made themselves felt out of proportion to their numbers. So as you look through the tariff you- will find that it lacks uniformity, it is full of inconsistencies and excrescences, and what this Bili proposes is to reduce it to scientific basis.
Now, in Canada I think we have outgrown the stage of this rough method of making tariffs. We have to take this legacy that has come down to us, and we will not perhaps treat that legacy with the respect which the junior member for Halifax might wish that we should use. We intend to take that legacy and to apply new methods, new rules, in order to make the tariff apply with equal benefit to all the people of Canada. Now that Canada has reached her present size we must admit that she has outgrown the old rough-and-ready method of making tariffs, and I think we must be prepared to adopt a (scientific process with our tariff, we in parliament must be prepared to apply all along the line, consistently and fearlessly, some definite policy that the majority of this House can stand for. What we ask by this commission is that they will collect for us the facts, not opinions, not theories, but facts, and on those facts we, in the exercise of our reason and judgment, will be able to base a tariff measure which we will not be unprepared to submit to the whole people of Canada.
Now I regard this Bill as a long step in advance. I consider that the government have acted fearlessly and courageously, they have shown initiative in bringing down this measure that the House is called upon to deal with. Furthermore, this Bill fulfils a repeated promise on the part of our chief, and a promise that many of us have made on the platforms of the country from one end to the other. I do not wonder that the hon. 'member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) was somewhat surprised that this new government, within four or five months of its creation, should actually set to work to implement the promises that were given to the electorate. That is not the experience of the .other side, I admit, but that is what this government is intending to do, and here is the first instalment of the fulfilment of those deliberate promises.
There are a few more to fulfil, however.

They will be fulfilled more rapidly than promises have been in the past 15 years. What is proposed by this legislation is primarily to create an impartial non-partisan commission, and that com-

mission should busy itself in a scientific manner in getting at established facts, then those facts will be submitted to parliament, and upon these facts legislation will be based.
To say that this measure violates constitutional practice is to indulge in one of those sophistries in which these hon. gentlemen often indulge when addressing this House. There is not one privilege'that this House at the present time enjoys, not one privilege that the opposition has hitherto enjoyed, that would be infringed upon in the slightest degree by this measure. Do you suppose that we are going to ask the Tariff Commission to prepare our next tariff Bill? Not at all. We do not even intend to ask them to make any recommendation. They are to give us the exact facts with regard to existing conditions, and the ministry will take upon themselves the full responsibility, and the members of this House will take upon themselves the full responsibility which they have to take in the application and use that they make of these facts. This is nothing unusual. We have it in everyday life. A judge sits upon the bench, he wants to know about some technical matter, about a building, perhaps, that has collapsed, what does he do? He names some man who is an expert in building, this man examines the building, and in this way he establishes the facts. Does that in any way impinge upon the dignity of the bench or interfere with the status of the court? By no means, but the judge has the facts placed before him, and upon those facts he gives his judgment.
I am of the opinion that when this measure comes to be understood it will receive the well deserved commendation of all classes throughout Canada. It will, I think, receive the commendation of the producer, of the man who will come to this parliament and ask that he be given a certain degree of protection in the shape of a duty upon that which he has to sell. If he can prove that he is entitled to that protection he will receive it, but if he cannot prove that he is entitled to it he will probably find that the protection which he presently enjoys will be diminished. The only way in which that can be accomplished is by having before us the necessary statement of facts. I want to point out that when we speak of the producer in this country we include the farmer just as much as the man who runs.the factory. Almost everybody in this country is a producer, and each man who is a producer will naturally enjoy the benefits that must accrue from this Act. Read the definition at the beginning of the Act. Goods are treated of throughout the whole Act, and what do goods include? They include pro-844	*	'	-	|
ducts of the farm, horses, cattle and other animals, and everything mat the farmer
produces is just as likely to be sub' jected to the inquiry of this commission in the interest of the farmer as are the goods which the manufacturers themselves produce. Now, take the consumer. I mean the class of consumers who are broad enough and big enough Canadians to live and let live. I do not mean the class of consumer wno insists upon having everything he produces protected, and everything he consumes free. I do not mean that class, they are not in the majority in Canada to-day, and I hope they never will be. But I refer to the consumer who is a big enough and broad enough Canadian to say: I am willing that what I consume shall be, to a slight extent, increased in price in order that there may be built up throughout the length and breadth of Canada diversified industry, and in order that the Canadian people may not be reduced to the position of hewers of wood and drawers of water. It is very much to the advantage of the consumer that he should' know whether he is being overcharged in the price he has to pay, and I believe that when the consumer realizes that there is an impartial commission created to investigate such matters on his behalf, and ascertain whether he is overcharged for what he purchases he will say: That is what I want.
It seems to me that this Bill commends itself to the industrial worker as: well. He is both producer and consumer. He probably pays a little more for what he consumes, but he is protected hr what he produces in the industrial, establishments' of this country, and as he reads this Bill he will see that it provides a means by which an investigation can he made as to whether he is securing a just and fair proportion of the selling price of that product to which his labour has contributed. That is what he wants to know. He wants to know whether he is getting an adequate proportion of the return which comes from the work of his hands, and he will have an opportunity to ascertain the facts when the provisions of this Bill go into operation. Therefore, he will say: I welcome this measure.
. The man who wishes to invest his capital in the industries of Canada, will he not find in the impartial report which this commission will present means of ascertaining whether our Canadian industrial enterprises are upon a sound and permanent basis? If, after he examines the reports, he is convinced, as I am sure he will be convinced, that they are worthy of his confidence, he will invest his money and we will, as a result of the publication oi such reports, bring into our country the money which we are so anxious to see invested in our industrial enterprises.

So, it seems to me that it is a good thing for the producer, the consumer, the industrial worker and the investor, and, that being the case, I can defend, and will be glad of the opportunity of defending on any platform in this country, the introduction and passage of the Bill that we now have before us. What we members of this House called upon to pass legislation, -want, is to know the real facts and the exact conditions as they exist in Canada before undertaking to deal with the tariff.
If I may be permitted to give advice to the government, I would suggest that, although the Bill does not designate what the qualifications of the commissioners are to be, there are some things that might be avoided in making their appointment. I think it would be a mistake to endeavour to outline in the Bill what class of men should be appointed as commissioners. You would probably limit the choice and I can assure you that to Secure men of the calibre that are required, you should limit the choice as little as possible. The whole Dominion of Canada is not too big a place in which to search for the very best men. I would not think it would be advisable that these three commissioners should be representatives of particular interests. Some one may say:	We should put a manufacturer
on; we should put a farmer on; wre should put a transportation man on, but these three, each representing a different interest, would tight their fellows for their own particular industry, or, to avoid a disagreement, would make a compromise whicii would be satisfactory to none. That is not what we want. We do not want the members of the commission to feel that they are there to represent a particular interest; we want them to feel that they are there to represent the people of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Nor, do we want technical experts. Sometimes we are told that this must be a board of technical experts. If you commence to name technical experts, you will soon find that you require a very large number of them. If a man is a technical expert in the matter of iron, for instance, he knows very little about woollen or cotton. He way be perfectly familiar with one article and know very little about other commodities. I do not think we want technical experts, men who have spent their whole lives dealing with a particular classification, because we have a great many different classifications and because, as a rule, men who are familiar with some particular article, are not able to take the broad view that is necessary of other businesses besides their own. If I may be permitted to offer advice to the ministers, I would say that they should not necessarily confine their choice to men Mr. AMES.
who have fought and bled for the Conservative party. I think that if there is any man in Canada who is eminently fitted for this position, he should not be rejected by reason of his previous political record. We want the biggest men we can get, but we *want men who are not out of sympathy with the policy that the party on this side of the House avowedly stands for. We want men who are not out of sympathy with the idea that protection, reasonably applied, is what Canada needs for her development. Let us have three big, broadminded Canadians, every one a man of administrative ability, who can organize and arrange the work and prepare the lines of investigation.
We want men of judicial capacity who can hold at arms-length the evidence that is placed before them and can correlate the various facts and part Them in their proper place. We -want men who earn determine and weight The value of evidence and who can eventually make reports to this House in which the statements made are properly and proportionately set out. Now', salaries such as are mentioned are not much for men of that size and character. You must admit that the salaries of the Cabinet ministers are too small, but the ministers have other honours that come to them, and I would hate to believe that it is the salaries that keep the ministers in their places. But, even the salaries that are mentioned in this Bill are none too large for men of the kind we want. If the government secures the sort of men we want I venture to say that there will not be one of them who will not be called upon to make a financial sacrifice when he enters the service upon these terms. If broadminded, fair-viewed men are chosen, and if they are given an- opportunity to make of this Tariff Commissi an what it can be made, I am sure they will win the confidence of the country, they will hold the confidence of the country, and they will be only too gladly continued in office by the present opposition, when, in the fair distant future, they have an opportunity of doing so.
This Tariff Commission is put under the direction cf the Minister of Finance, and that has been in some quarters criticised as inadvisable. Well, it seems to me the most natural and proper provision that could be made. Who else is there that is competent to generally direct the work that may be done by this commission? It will be impossible for them to take up 'all the schedules of the tariff at once; some one must tell them what work to begin upon; some one must guide them in the direction they are to follow, and it is natural and right they should be under the direction of that man in 'the

Cabinet who is charged by his fellows to look after the revenues of the country and who will have to introduce and defend any tariff legislation that will be submitted to this House. I sincerely hope that this Tariff Commission may be prompted to take up and continue this work in a systematic and useful manner. I hope the people do not imagine that the moment this board is created they can start an heterogeneous series of representations to the commission. The commission will probably take up the tariff schedule by schedule, and will study them systematically and will send for witnesses when they want them, and when a man is asked to come and give his testimony it will be after the commission have prepared themselves by advance knowledge to receive and properly value what may be told them. And after the tariff has once been carefully gone over and we have a library that will result from it, then that commission will continue to be a permanent commission because rectifications will always be necessary. Conditions are changing ini 'Canada from year to year, and it will be necessary to have a board that will understand the tariff thoroughly and which can receive applications and hear complaints and pass on recommendations, if they seem to be desirable.
Coming now to the duties of the commissioners-and I do not propose to take the Bill clause by clause, but simply to make a .sort of general sketch of the duties of the commissioners as I see them-it means that the commission is directly charged to make inquiries. To make inquiries into what? to make inquiries as to the facts and conditions as they exist in Canada and elsewhere. Now, from the point of view cf the Canadian producer, the Tariff Commission will inquire, first, as to the cost of raw material at the various points where the raw material is turned into manufactured products. The cost of raw material naturally indludes the cost of transportation to the place where it is used. Then they will study the cost of creating the raw material into the finished and marketable product. That will naturally include wages, superintendence, overhead charges, the cost of seilling, and some times the cost of carrying to the consumer, and it will include a legitimate interest on the money borrowed and a legitimate dividend on the actual money invested. These factors and many others all go into the cost, and it requires a scientific body to ascertain what the costs actually are. Next to that it will be necessary to ascertain what it costs to transport the product from the place where it is manufactured to tt ? place where it is consumed, an
expense which usually falls upon the consumer and an expense which it is necessary to know or otherwise we would not be able to ascertain whether the ultimate selling price was just and proper. Finally, as respects the producer, we have the right to know, and we intend to find out, just wihat the labour conditions are throughout Canada. I think we desire here in Canada to maintain a standard of living for our industrial workers that is in keeping with our Canadian civilization. The nations which compete with us so frequently for our home markets do not have the same standard of living as we do, and we do not wish to see our workingmen reduced to the condition of the workingmen in these countries. We therefore wish to know what it costs the workingman in Canada to live as he ought to live, what wages he is making in Canada and whether he is getting a fair share in the selling price of the manufactured article. Those things we ought to and shall know if this commission fulfils its purpose.
So much then from the point of view of the purchaser. The tariff commissioners will ascertain the cist ci the raw material and the assembling thereof; the cost of manufacture; the cost of transportation, and they will study the conditions of the industrial workers who are engaged in these productions. They go further, because in order that we may know how to equalize the cost of production as in foreign lands with our own, it will be necessary for them to prosecute their studies in the countries which compete for our home markets, and there also they will fully ascertain the cost of the raw material, the cost of manufacture, the cost of transportation and the labour conditions as they there exist. Then, when we have these facts for comparative purposes, we shall be able to judge what it will be necessary to put upon these commodities produced in Canada, Py way of a customs duty, in order to protect our home market, as against the producer elsewhere.
Now, taking up the Bill from the consumer's standpoint, this Tariff Commission purposes to carry on an investigation which certainly is in his interest and for his benefit. It purposes to ascertain what is ihe. selling price of the manufacturer, of ihe wholesaler or middleman, of the retail .merchant, in order to see whether in these successive stages the commodity is so enhanced in price that it reaches the ultimate consumer at a cost that is higher than is fair to him. Every circumstance and every condition that affects the ultimate selling price will be germane to the inquiry of this commission. If it should be alleged and shown that there be any [DOT]ombiue in restraint of trade which unduly enhances the price of the article*

to the consumer; if it should be shown that there are secret agreements between the various producers which advance the price beyond what was legitimate; if it should be shown that industries were endeavouring, on watered stock which represented no real assets, to pay dividends, and on account of this state of affairs trying to get an enhanced price from the consumer, that would be known. If there were excessive charges beyond such as were reasonable and right, saddled upon the product, and attempted to be taken <ut of the consumer in the ultimate purchase price that would be germane to this inquiry. If there was discrimination, if there were rebates in railway rates; ia fact if there was any circumstance or condition which might unduly or unfairly enhance the price of the article, eventually to the consumer, every one of these circumstances might be legitimately studied and reported upon by this commission.
If the price is found to be artificially enhanced, the claim for protection would to that extent be vitiated, and the facts brought before this House would enable this House to put the penalty where it belonged. If I were a member of the opposition, it seems to me that I would not ask for the creation of any better instrument than this to enable me to get at the actual facts of the case from the consumer's point of view. When you get the reports of these commissioners, as you will from time to time, and have a chance to read them, you can determine the lines of action; and, with everything uncovered, I cannot see where it will be possible for any injustice to remain in our tariff.
This commission has also the right to deal with other matters that may be referred to it from time to time by the government. Any other matter relating to trade ot commerce will be proper work for the commission. There is a special clause to enable the board to meet emergencies that may from time to time arise. I suppose it will apply to trade treaties Last session when we were called on to discuss the all-important question of reciprocity with the United States, the members of the United States Senate and the House of Representatives had in their hands voluminous reports containing a complete study of the conditions prevailing on both sides of the line with the relative cost of production in Canada and the United States. They went into the discussion prepared at every point. But what had we? What did the civil service officials spoken of by the hon. member for Halifax give us? Did they give us any carefully prepared statistics? They gave us absolutely nothing that we could not have picked out of the blue-books for Mr. AMES.
ourselves. We went into that discussion dependent on United States Senate and House of Representatives for information and if we had not been able to see ourselves as others see us, we would never have succeeded in convincing the people of Canada that the bargain was for us an unwise one.
We were discussing the other day trade relations with Australia. When the government may have a measure on that subject ready to submit to this House, what more profitable than that they should ask the Tariff Commission to ascertain what would be the probable effect upon Canada of an arrangement such as proposed. That I take it is the class of special subjects which will be from time to time referred to the Tariff Commission.
Now, some objections have been raised to this measure. I do not attach much importance to the constitutional objection. We have heard a great deal about Royal commissions. This is not a Royal commission in the ordinary sense. "A Royal commission is a temporary body appointed to investigate some specific subject, and as soon as it makes its report and findings, it is dismissed, because its work is done. This commission is not of that character. It is a permanent body which we hope will be continued from year to year, and it will not make findings in the way Royal commissions usually do.
It has been objected in some quarters that we propose to endow this commission with inquisitorial power. That in a sense is true. The commissions will have power to summon witnesses, to order them to bring their books and papers, to examine them under oath, even to inquire into a man's private business. It will have power to compel witnesses to attend, though I do not suppose it will ever have to resort to that. It has not been so in the United States. The Tariff Board there has never had any difficulty in getting the producers to come and give it all the information it desired. It is proposed to put the burden of proof on the man who asks for protection. He will have to prove that he is entitled to have his request complied with, otherwise lie will not get it. On that point let me quote from the address of Professor H. C. Emery, the Chairman of the Tariff Board of the United1 States:
If, however, the principle should be firmly established that -a protective tariff, however necessary or desirable, is none the less a favour, and that the burden of proof rests upon the producer to show cause why such protection should be granted, the matter of power (to examine books, &c.) becomes relatively unimportant.
You have only to say to the producer, 'if you are not prepared to give us the evidence to show why we should give you pro-

tection, do not wonder if we do not give you what you ask lor.' Under these conditions people will be only too glad to give us the fullest possible information. It is possible that the Tariff Commission may from time to time find it necessary to secure confidential information which they mav not see fit to put verbatim into the evidence, because it must be remembered that in that way they will have greater freedom and get nearly at ithe facts-inasmuch as men will speak freely when they feel that they are not going to give their competitors in the same line of business al the inside information in regard to their own particular enterprise. That is only legitimate and right.
The Bill provides thai the commissioners shall report through the Finance Minister to the Governor in Council. That again seems to me right and proper. It must be remembered that the government, on the findings of fact from this commission, wilr be called upon to frame their Tariff Bill. There is absolutely no attempt to evade any ministerial responsibility by this arrangement. I do not anticipate that any Tariff Board will ever prepare a Bill, or recommend that the duty be 25 or 30 or 40 per cent on specific articles. They are required onlj to inquire into questions of fact as to the real conditions-existing here and elsewhere. When their evidence and findings ha/ve 'been placed in the hands of the government, the cabinet, more especially the Finance Minister, will determine what form the Tariff Bill will take; and after it has been submitted by the Finance Minister to his colleagues and been approved by them, the Bill, together with the evidence on which it is based, will be brought by the government to the House and will become the property of the House. Every member of the opposition will then have an opportunity to go over the evidence and judge for himself whether 20 or 25 or 30 per cent is the proper rate of duty based upon the facts disclosed. If I were a member of the opposition I would ask nothing better than that I might have the facts before me, admitted by both sides, and then I could hold the government to follow lines that are reasonable and right. _ One more feature strikes one in connection with this commission which is to be commended, that is, the endeavour to make the body as far as possible a permanent one. It is appointed for five years, and the hope is implied if not expressed that the members who are appointed in the first instance will, if they make good, go on for a further term of five years. They are made eligible for re-appointment, which implies that it is -hoped that they will accept reappointment. Men should go into this work expecting to make it their life-work, and I hope they will continue in it
for many years, even though administrations may come and go.
There are some things which cannot be put into the Bill which it seems to me will fall naturally within the -scope of this Tariff Commission. One thing, I think, would be to make a glossary or dictionary of the tariff, so that we would have it in plain language and would know what the items meant, and the customs officials along the border would -all interpret a definition in -the same way.
Another thing which the commission -might do would be -to establish a customs museum in which we would have samples of the various articles mentioned in the schedules, so that they could be seen and handled by our customs officials who would thus learn how to distinguish and classify them. It might even be possible for this Tariff Commission to assume eventually more or les-s civil service qualifications and exercise educational functions. To whom could we better give the duty of determining what candidates were best qualified to enter the customs service, and the best means of preparing and training, men to enter the higher grades of that service? Iiua great man yways this -commission could render extremely useful service outside the ordinary lines of this Bill.
The conditions in Canada in 1912 are vastly different from those in 1896. Our revenue has grown until it is three times as great and -our -customs receipts a,re four times -as large as they were 15 years -ago. The unscientific methods whi-ch were good enough for Canada in her (boyhood and eaady manhood are not good enough from 1912 onwards. We want something better, -and we think we have found the way -to get it. Tllie experience -of busy ministers in the past has been spoken of to-night. Well, we had Mr. Fielding, Mr. Paterson and Mr. Brodeur, ministers in the late government, making peripatetic voyages throughout Canada, stopping at different places and taking evidence. Every theorist, every crank, every inveterate free trader of the English school, every man who had something to say appeared before them and gave his evidence. There was the most heterogeneous conglomeration -of evidence collected that one could possibly imagine. It was all typewritten and filled s-everal Saratoga trunks, and I venture to say that no-t one of the -ministers -ever read i-t through. We have ample evidence of	that in the fact that
Mr. Fielding, after he brought in his Tariff Bill to the House, made upwards of one hundred changes in it, showing that he had not very thoroughly digested the matter submitted to him. Should we call on our ministers to make such an experiment again? It is evidently impossible

for ministers, if they are to properly manage their departments, to have sufficient time at their disposal to travel through the country taking evidence or to sit down and discuss tariff matters with every one who has theories on the subject. We ought not to ask our ministers to do that, and we are seeking to appoint a commission who will collate the facts and submit them to the ministers who in their turn will lay them before the House. What we want is the truth and nothing else. Those who are accused of advocating high protection want nothing but what they are entitled to. The fullest possible light that can be thrown on the business of those who claim protection will be furnished, and if it be found that, under that scrutiny, their pretensions do not hojd good, this House will know it, and will withdraw any excessive benefits in the way of protection to which these people are not entitled.
In closing let me emphasize this fact. This commission, which is to be appointed, will be charged to investigate facts and conditions. They will not take on themselves the duties of ministers or of members of parliament. They are not going to prepare any Tariff Act. They will not make any recommendation such as that Isuoh an article shall be protected to the extent of 25 or 30 per cent. That will not be their duty. Every prerogative enjoyed by the ministers and members of this House will remain absolutely unimpaired when this Act passes. We shall be called on to exercise our judgment and best faculties in determining what shall be the tariff duty just as before. The only difference will be that we shall no longer be groping our way in the dark.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. W. KYTE (Richmond, Nova Scotia).
speechtext:
It must be perfectly manifest that we are on the eve of another great struggle between the two classes-'the high protectionists and the moderate protectionists. My hon. friend from St. Antoine Mr. Ames), was not speaking ten minutes before hie repeated the statement three times that the consumer may suffer an increase in the price of the goods he consumes by reason of the appointment of this commission. He further made the statement that the tariff at present shows the pressure ot the clamour of consumers who make much more noise than their numbers justify. I must congratulate the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) on the frankness with which he discussed this- question. Knowing, as we do, the interests which he controls in this country, we would be very much surprised if he took a different stand. This government is doing very well in the way of appointing commissions to relieve themselves of responsibility. They -are not very Mr. AMES.
long in power, but during the few months they have been in office they have appointed commissions by the dozen. The principle of adequate protection, as it was defined by the right hon. the First Minister (Mr. Borden), seems to have had its reincarnation about the year 1907. I would ask permission to quote from the ' Canadian Manufacturer ' of May 17, 1907, an article which is interesting in view of the present conditions:
, Mr. R. L. Borden, leader of the Conservative opposition, in the Dominion House of Commons, will, it is stated, in a few days, tour Ontario and other provinces and address publio gatherings on the important issues of the day; and it is expected that some of the Conservative members of Ontario will accompany him for speech making purposes.
_ Whatever the other important political issues may be which Mr. Borden and his friends may discuss before the electorate, it is to be most ardently hoped that the question of tariff protection will not he neglected hut kept well to the front, and we also hope that from this time on not only the Conservative speakers, but the Liberal orators also, will not fail to inform the people on that subject.
Mr. Borden entered parliament in 1896, just after the defeat of the late Conservative government, which, because of their having attached greater importance to other issues than tariff protection, forfeited the prestige of their party and went into opposition. Perhaps they thought that other issues were of more importance to their party and to the country than that which had placed them in power. Those issues might have been considered of greater importance, but while attention was given to these, that of protection should not have been neglected as it was, with the result that such protection as we have since had, as exemplified in the tariff, is administered from a hostile standpoint. It may be that Mr. Borden and his friends are staunch protectionists; it is to be hoped that they are, but during the entire session of the Dominion parliament so recently ended, we do not remember any occasion of pronounced and vigorous speeches having been in favour of the policy of tariff protection, either by Mr. Borden or any of his lieutenants. On some occasions something may have been said, hut they were of a perfunctory character, in which no particular ardour was shown. Many grand opportunities have occurred during the discussion having reference to the adoption of the proposition of the Finance Minister, hut ' Hansard ' fails to record any elaborate and telling arguments in favour of protection by Mr. Borden or liis friends, such as thrilled the members and the country under the regime of Sir John.
This remarkable lack of sympathy and enthusiasm was a result, without doubt, of the peculiar stand taken by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association at their Halifax convention in 1802, and before and since that occasion, when the association and the country were assured that the tariff had been taken out of politics

that if any difference of opinion existed, they were regarding the administration of the tariff, all being agreed that
2658

protection in some sliape or other had come to stay. Canadian manufacturers and the believers in protection throughout the country, a great and powerful element that had been able to make the National Policy an unbounded success, found themselves, Sampson like, the victims of a deceitful Delilah.
Are Canadian manufacturers-are the people of Canada who are believers in protection, to have this valuable belonging restored to them? Who is to restore it? When is it to be done? How is it to be done? Will the Conservative party under the leadership of Mr. Borden or of any other man undertake the job? Talk is cheap. What is wanted is men of action who will be up and doing. Who are they to be?
From the Bill which Las been submitted this afternoon and the stand taken by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), there is no longer any doubt in the public mind as to who the people axe, who will give high protection to Canadian manufactures so long as they remain in power. The Prime Minister made the statement that the government had not received any request from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association for the adoption of this measure. It is perfectly manifest to the hon. gentleman as it must be to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association was not likely to go to the government to extract any promise as to their policy with respect to protection; they would rather come to them to require the fulfillment of promises made before the elections, made by the party led by the Prime Minister before the government was formed; made, I have no doubt, before the Minister of Finance was so unexpectedly called to the high position in the government that he occupies at the present time. There was no political communion; no sympathic affiliation between the Finance Minister and the Prime Minister except on the question of the interests, and I think I am not doing the Minister of Finance any injustice, when I say that it was well understood throughout Canada that he was to represent the interests in the government of the present day. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association met in Montreal some weeks after the elections, and if I am not mistaken, among the resolutions they passed on that occasion, was one in favour ot a Tariff Commission,-presumably for the purpose of ' taking the tariff out of polities.' I was somewhat at a loss to understand how, under our principles of constitutional government, a Tariff Commission could take the tariff out of politics.
' But the Minister of Finance has dispelled any doubt existing in my mind as to that point, because he has frankly stated that the tariff will not be taken out of politics by this measure. We on this side are thankful for his frank statement. The junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) pointed out how impossible it is for the
government to relieve itself in respect to its responsibility for the Tariff. What is the object and purpose of the Bill? They appoint a Commission to inquire as to conditions in respect to tariff matters for the purpose M reaching a conclusion as to whether or not protection should be increased in this, that, or the other direction. _ When the government brings down its tariff measure in the future, and they are charged with giving a certain industry too much protection, the answer probably will be: We have done- this on the report of the Tariff Commission which was appointed for the purpose of instructing and advising us as to the amount of protection these interests need.
If the hon. member (Mr. Kyte) will allow a question, I would like to ask what difference there would be between that and the recommendation of experts?

That was well explained by my hon. friend from Halifax; and I think if the hon. member for Peterboro (Mr. Burnham) will take the time to read the speech of my hon. friend, he will see his question answered. My hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) intimated that the Tariff Commission should not be made up of men out of sympathy with the principles for which the government stand. That is another intimation that the tariff commission will be selected from the ranks of the high protectionists. I am sure it is not necessary for us to have that statement from the hon. gentleman in order to reach a conclusion on that point. Up to the present time, the government has been called upon to appoint many persons to office. Some positions have been opened, some have been created; and the government, during the last three months have busied themselves with the work of making appointments. In no case have they gone outside the ranks of their own party to fill a position. Even in the case of a postoffice with a salary of $35 a year, they do not go outside of the ranks of their party to fill the place. If they, in the case of a post office with ia salary of $35 a year are so mindful of their party interests that they will not allow even a small position to escape them, we can easily understand what will happen in the case of appointing men to positions at $7,000 a year. I am also reminded that, in cases where they are called upon to fill positions, they are not even limited in their choice to the electors of Canada, but go outside these ranks and appoint females to offices, as was done recently in the county of Ri-mouski.
The Bill provides that the Tariff Commission shall summon before them such people as they desire to give evidence, but it contains no provision under which

a person can go before the com-imittee voluntarily to (present his views. Taking the authority of	the	hon.
member for St. Antoine, we know that the commission will consist of high protectionists. We know that they are perfectly aware of the sympathies and sentiments of 'the government that appoints them, and they will naturally go for their advice to those who are in sympathy with those interests and conditions. But should a representative of the consuming classes desire to give evidence, there is no provision by which he can go before the commission voluntarily for that purpose. There are in this country two classes-the consumers and the manufacturers; and this country has been divided for many years between these two classes and will continue to be so divided. I aver that it is absolutely unfair to the consumers to give such large and important powers to one class of the community to the exclusion of the other class. We have in this country the division between capital and labour. ' When questions arise involving the interests of these parties, boards of conciliation are asked for to adjust these differences. Would it not be preposterous to imagine that in selecting such a board of conciliation, only the representatives of capital should be appointed on the board? If such a thing were attempted by the government, there would be such a cry all over this country against the manifest injustice of it, that the government would not dare to renew the attempt. But we know that differences will arise between the consumers and the^manufacturers; and the government, by their Bill, and by the policy which they have announced and defended in the past, will have only representatives of the manufacturers upon this Tariff Board, so that only that side of the question will be enquired into.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kyte) tell me in what section of the Bill he finds that provision?

the present time a proposition to extend our trade with Australia and the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) I understand, will go to that far off colony in the near future, for the purpose of interviewing the government with a view to increasing our trade with them. The mission of the Minister of Trade and Commerce is analogous to that of the commission that w'as to be appointed by the Imperial Conference, but it has no analogy whatever with the commission that is now under consideration. The question of tariff and the question of extending trade are entirely different things, so much so, that they are almost contradictory. For instance, when we are seeking to enlarge our trade with 'another country, we do not start by increasing our tariff against the products of that country. We had an opportunity of extending our trade in the direction of the United States a year ago, when the people of the United States showed a desire to increase their trade with us. What'did they do? Did they increase their tariff against our goods? No, they took the duties off our goods, to enable them to get into their market free of duty. Therefore, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this question of a commission for the purpose of enlarging our trade between different parts of the empire is an entirely different proposition from the one before the House at the present time.
I have listened up to the present time with the greatest interest to the hon. gentlemen who have spoken in support of the Bill. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) made a fair and frank statement, one which is perfectly intelligible to any person who desires to get the same grasp of the principles of the Bill which he himself possessed. The right hon. the Prime Minister did not go into the principle of the Bill any further than to make a defence for the government in attempting to delegate the powers that they really should exercise to the commission proposed. The hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), has gone further and he has stated the case for the protectionists of this country. Up to the present time we have not had any speeches from hon. gentlemen representing the farming communities in the west. I sincerely hope that before this debate is closed we will hear the views of hon. members on the government side representing Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta in respect to this Bill. I may not be correctly informed as to the sentiments of the people in that part of Canada but my judgment is that they are hostile to any proposal on the part of the government looking to a further increase in the tariff duties. I will await with interest the view taken by hon. gentlemen representing these provinces on the government side of the House, but whether or not the gentle-
Mr. KYTE
men from these provinces are in favour of or against the Bill, I speak for those consumers in the eastern part of Canada whose interests will be injured and whose prosperity in the future will be greatly hampered if the policy of protection, enunciated by the hon. member- for Montreal, St. Antoine, is carried into effect. As far as they are concerned, there is no doubt as to where they stand on this important question, and, feeling as I do, I have no hesitation in recording my vote m what I believe to be their interests.

Mr. Speaker, as the hour is somewhat late, as it has been intimated that there are five members on this side of the House as well as five on the other who are yet to speak, and as we were here until after twelve o'clock last night, I move the adjournment of the debate.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
